title: Cell Biology and the Chemistry of Life
tagline: A guided tour of the cell and the four families of molecules that build it.
overview: The content follows the standard first-year cell biology sequence, anchored in chemistry. It begins with the scale and architecture of cells, then introduces carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids as molecules with structure and function, and moves on to membranes, the endomembrane system and cytoskeleton, mitochondria and chloroplasts, cell signalling, and finally the cell cycle, division and death. Each unit is written to prepare the reader for Level 3 courses in metabolism, gene expression, biomolecule chemistry and recombinant DNA technology.
whyItMatters: Everything in Level 3 happens somewhere inside a cell, in a compartment, on a membrane or on a molecule. If you can picture where the ribosome, the mitochondrion and the receptor are and what they are made of, enzyme kinetics, metabolic pathways, transcription and cloning stop being abstract diagrams and become events in a place you know.
studyTips: Draw a cell from memory every week and add one more detail each time (organelle, membrane protein, pathway); the act of drawing exposes what you do not yet know.
For every molecule family, learn the monomer, the bond that joins monomers, and one example of structure determining function; that three-part template transfers to nearly every exam question.
Think in scales: before you answer a question, say whether it concerns nanometres (molecules), micrometres (organelles and cells) or millimetres (tissues).
Use the animation and structure tools (Inner Life of the Cell, PDB-101, AlphaFold) to look at the same objects from several angles; seeing a real structure makes textbook cartoons meaningful.

units.title: What Is a Cell? Types, Scale and Architecture
units.hook: A single bacterium is about the width of a mitochondrion; a human cell is large enough to hold thousands of bacteria; a protein is a thousand times smaller than the cell around it. Getting a feeling for these scales is the first step to understanding why cells are built the way they are.
learningObjectives: State the main points of cell theory and the evidence behind it.
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and place Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya in the three-domain scheme.
Order common biological objects by size, from atoms to organisms, with typical dimensions.
Explain why cell size is limited using the surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Describe what light, fluorescence and electron microscopy can and cannot resolve.

keyConcepts.definition: All living organisms consist of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of structure and function, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
A cell with no membrane-bound nucleus; DNA lies in a nucleoid region, ribosomes are 70S, and cells are typically 1 to 5 micrometres across (Bacteria and Archaea).
A cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and internal organelles, 80S ribosomes in the cytosol, and typical diameters of 10 to 100 micrometres.
Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, a classification based on ribosomal RNA comparisons by Woese and colleagues; Archaea are prokaryotes that are, molecularly, closer to eukaryotes in several respects.
A specialised, often membrane-bounded compartment inside a eukaryotic cell, such as the nucleus, mitochondrion or Golgi apparatus.
For a sphere of radius r the ratio is 3/r, so as a cell grows its surface (which supplies materials) falls behind its volume (which consumes them), limiting size.
The smallest distance at which two points can be told apart; a light microscope is limited to about 200 nm, while electron microscopes resolve well below 1 nm.
The cytosol is the fluid part of the cell's interior; the cytoplasm is the cytosol plus the organelles, excluding the nucleus.

deeper.beginner: Cells are the smallest units that count as alive. All of them have a membrane around them, DNA as genetic material, and ribosomes to make proteins. Bacteria are the simplest cells and have no nucleus; animal and plant cells are larger and are divided into compartments called organelles, each with its own job. To get a feel for scale: an atom is about 0.1 nm, a protein 5 nm, a virus 100 nm, a bacterium 1 micrometre, a human cell 10 to 20 micrometres.
deeper.intermediate: The reason cells are small is geometric: nutrients enter through the surface, but the metabolic demand grows with volume. For r = 1 micrometre, surface area to volume is 3 per micrometre; for r = 10 micrometres it is 0.3 per micrometre, ten times worse. Eukaryotes solve this by adding internal membranes and compartments, which also separate chemical environments (for example the acidic lysosome from the neutral cytosol). The three-domain tree emerged from small-subunit rRNA sequences; Archaea resemble bacteria in cell organisation but resemble eukaryotes in their transcription and replication machinery. Imaging has trade-offs: light microscopy can watch living cells but is limited to 200 nm; fluorescence adds molecular specificity; electron microscopy resolves membranes and ribosomes but needs fixed, non-living samples.
deeper.advanced: The prokaryote versus eukaryote dichotomy is increasingly seen as a simplification: some bacteria have internal membrane systems and protein-bounded compartments, and eukaryotes arose from a symbiotic merger in which an archaeal host acquired a bacterial endosymbiont (which became the mitochondrion). Quantities per cell are surprisingly well constrained: a typical mammalian cell volume of about 2000 cubic micrometres holds on the order of 10^9 to 10^10 proteins by modern estimates, and such numbers are checked against concentration, density and mass constraints (as the BioNumbers resource encourages). Super-resolution microscopy (STORM, PALM, STED) overcomes the diffraction limit by controlling when molecules fluoresce, achieving resolutions of tens of nanometres in living specimens.

commonMistakes: Saying prokaryotes 'have no organelles at all'; they lack membrane-bound organelles, but have ribosomes, a nucleoid and in some cases protein-bound compartments.
Treating the cell wall and the cell membrane as the same thing; plants, fungi and bacteria have walls outside the membrane, while animal cells have no wall.
Confusing magnification with resolution; magnifying further does not reveal more detail if the optics cannot resolve it.
Assuming bigger cells are always better; the surface-area-to-volume limit is real.

selfCheck.question: Which feature is found in all prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
selfCheck.explanation: All cells make proteins on ribosomes. A nucleus and mitochondria are eukaryotic features, and animal cells lack a cell wall.

selfCheck.question: A spherical cell grows from radius 1 micrometre to radius 10 micrometres. Its surface-area-to-volume ratio changes by what factor?
selfCheck.explanation: Surface area to volume equals 3/r for a sphere, so a ten-fold increase in radius reduces the ratio ten-fold, from 3 to 0.3 per micrometre.

selfCheck.question: Roughly which of these objects is smallest?
selfCheck.explanation: A ribosome is about 20 to 25 nm across, a mitochondrion is on the order of 1 micrometre long, a bacterium 1 to 5 micrometres, and a red blood cell about 7 to 8 micrometres.

units.title: Carbohydrates and Lipids: Fuel, Structure and Membranes
units.hook: A cotton shirt and a potato are both polymers of glucose, yet one resists digestion while the other is food. The difference lies in a single orientation of one bond, a fact that shows how much biology is hidden in chemical detail.
learningObjectives: Classify carbohydrates as monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides, and draw the open-chain and ring forms of glucose.
Distinguish alpha from beta glycosidic linkages and relate them to starch, glycogen and cellulose.
Describe the structure of fatty acids, triglycerides, phospholipids and sterols.
Explain how saturation and chain length affect lipid behaviour and membrane fluidity.
Explain why fats store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

keyConcepts.definition: A simple sugar with formula (CH2O)n, such as glucose, fructose and ribose; classified as aldose or ketose and by carbon number.
The covalent bond joining two sugars through an oxygen atom, formed by condensation (loss of water); the alpha or beta orientation at carbon 1 matters.
Glucose polymers: starch (plant storage, alpha-1,4 with alpha-1,6 branches), glycogen (animal storage, more highly branched) and cellulose (structural, beta-1,4, linear chains).
A long hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid; saturated chains have no C=C bonds, unsaturated chains have one or more, usually cis, which introduce kinks.
Glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds; the main energy-storage lipid.
A glycerol (or sphingosine) backbone carrying two fatty-acid tails and a phosphate-containing polar head; amphipathic, so it forms bilayers.
A lipid with a four-ring skeleton; cholesterol is the main animal sterol, inserted into membranes where it modulates fluidity and is the precursor of steroid hormones.
Polymers are built by removing water between monomers and broken down by adding water; the same logic applies to all four macromolecule families.

deeper.beginner: Carbohydrates are sugars and chains of sugars. Glucose is the cell's main fuel, and cells store it as glycogen (animals) or starch (plants). Cellulose, built from the same glucose, is the tough material of plant cell walls. Lipids are oily or fatty molecules that do not mix with water: fats store energy, phospholipids build membranes, and cholesterol helps adjust membrane stiffness.
deeper.intermediate: Glucose (C6H12O6) mostly exists as a six-membered ring in water, in which carbon 1 can point down (alpha) or up (beta). Linking glucose units alpha-1,4 gives helical, digestible starch and glycogen, while beta-1,4 produces straight chains that pack side by side with hydrogen bonds into cellulose fibres, which human enzymes cannot cleave. Fats deliver about 37 kJ/g (9 kcal/g) compared with about 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g) for carbohydrates, because their carbon is more reduced and they are stored without water. Cis double bonds put a kink in a fatty acid, preventing tight packing; this lowers the melting point and increases membrane fluidity. Cholesterol stiffens membranes at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature.
deeper.advanced: Carbohydrates carry information as well as energy: glycans on proteins and lipids (glycoproteins, glycolipids) form the cell's 'sugar code', as in ABO blood groups, whose antigens differ by terminal sugars, and in lectin-mediated recognition and immune signalling. Lipid chemistry is much more diverse than the introductory classes suggest; classification systems such as LIPID MAPS list eight categories (fatty acyls, glycerolipids, glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, sterol lipids, prenol lipids, saccharolipids, polyketides). Lipids also act as signals: eicosanoids and phosphoinositides regulate inflammation and signalling. Because membrane lipid composition is tuned to temperature and function (homeoviscous adaptation), organisms alter fatty-acid saturation when the environment changes.

commonMistakes: Believing that starch and cellulose differ in their monomers; both are glucose polymers, differing in linkage geometry.
Describing unsaturated fatty acids as having no double bonds; saturated chains lack C=C, unsaturated ones have them.
Thinking cholesterol is only harmful; it is an essential membrane component and the precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids.
Drawing glucose as a flat hexagon; the ring is puckered and the alpha/beta distinction is about the orientation of the hydroxyl on carbon 1.

selfCheck.question: What is the key structural difference between starch and cellulose?
options: Starch is made from fructose; cellulose from glucose
Starch has alpha-1,4 glucose linkages; cellulose has beta-1,4 linkages
Cellulose is branched; starch is linear
selfCheck.explanation: Both are glucose polymers, but the alpha-1,4 linkage makes starch helical and digestible by amylase, whereas beta-1,4 links make straight chains that humans cannot hydrolyse.

selfCheck.question: Why do cis double bonds in fatty acids increase membrane fluidity?
options: They add hydrogen bonds between chains
They introduce kinks that prevent tight packing of acyl chains
They make the head groups more charged
selfCheck.explanation: A cis double bond bends the hydrocarbon chain, so neighbouring lipids cannot pack as closely, which lowers the melting point and keeps the bilayer fluid.

selfCheck.question: What type of bond joins a fatty acid to glycerol in a triglyceride?
selfCheck.explanation: The carboxyl group of each fatty acid forms an ester linkage with a hydroxyl group of glycerol, releasing water in a condensation reaction.

units.title: Proteins: Amino Acids, Structure and Folding
units.hook: A protein is made as a floppy chain, yet within seconds it folds into a precise shape that determines everything it does. In 1973 Christian Anfinsen showed that the instructions for that shape are written in the amino acid sequence itself, and in 2020 to 2021 computers finally learned to read them.
learningObjectives: Draw the general structure of an amino acid and classify the 20 standard side chains by chemistry.
Describe the peptide bond and the direction (N to C) of a polypeptide.
Explain primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure and the interactions that stabilise each.
Explain Anfinsen's experiment, the role of chaperones, and the consequences of misfolding.
Describe how denaturation and mutation alter protein function.

keyConcepts.definition: A central carbon bearing an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable side chain (R); at pH 7 the amino acid exists as a zwitterion.
Non-polar (for example Leu, Val, Phe), polar uncharged (Ser, Thr, Asn, Gln, Cys, Tyr), acidic (Asp, Glu) and basic (Lys, Arg, His); the side chain decides where a residue sits in the folded protein.
The amide bond between the carboxyl carbon of one residue and the amino nitrogen of the next, formed by condensation; planar with partial double-bond character.
Local regular folding stabilised by backbone hydrogen bonds: the alpha helix (3.6 residues per turn) and beta sheet (strands side by side).
The overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide, stabilised by a hydrophobic core, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and, in secreted proteins, disulfide bonds.
The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits into one complex, as in haemoglobin (four subunits).
A protein that helps others fold correctly by shielding hydrophobic regions and preventing aggregation, without becoming part of the final structure.
Loss of native three-dimensional structure by heat, extreme pH or chemicals, usually with loss of function, without breaking peptide bonds.

deeper.beginner: Proteins are chains of amino acids. There are 20 kinds, and each has a different side chain: some love water, some avoid it, some are charged. The order of amino acids in the chain determines how it folds into a specific 3D shape, and that shape determines its job, such as an enzyme, a structural fibre or a receptor. Heat or acid can unfold a protein, which is why cooking an egg changes it permanently.
deeper.intermediate: The chain has a backbone (N-C-alpha-C repeated) and side chains that point out. Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups produce alpha helices (i to i+4 bonding) and beta sheets (parallel or antiparallel strands). Tertiary structure is dominated by the hydrophobic effect: non-polar side chains bury themselves in the core while polar and charged ones face water. Cysteines in the oxidising environment outside cells can form disulfide bonds. Anfinsen unfolded ribonuclease A with urea and a reducing agent, then removed them and saw activity return, showing that the sequence alone specifies the native fold under the right conditions. In cells chaperones such as Hsp70 and GroEL help avoid aggregation, and misfolding underlies diseases such as Alzheimer's (amyloid) and prion disorders.
deeper.advanced: The Levinthal paradox points out that a chain cannot find its native state by sampling every conformation; folding proceeds down a funnel-shaped energy landscape with partially structured intermediates. The Ramachandran plot shows that steric hindrance restricts the backbone phi and psi angles to a few allowed regions, consistent with the observed secondary structures. Folding stability is marginal, typically 20 to 60 kJ/mol net, the small difference of large opposing enthalpy and entropy terms, so single mutations can destabilise a protein. Structure prediction advanced dramatically with AlphaFold 2, which predicts structures of single chains with accuracy comparable to experiment in many cases, but predicts a static structure and does not by itself describe dynamics, folding pathways or the effect of mutations on stability.

commonMistakes: Saying a denatured protein has broken peptide bonds; denaturation disrupts non-covalent interactions and folded structure, not the backbone.
Thinking disulfide bonds are the main force holding proteins together; the hydrophobic core and hydrogen bonds contribute far more, and many cytosolic proteins have no disulfides.
Mixing up levels: the alpha helix is secondary structure, not tertiary, even though it is 3D.
Assuming one sequence gives one rigid shape; many proteins have flexible or disordered regions that matter for function.

selfCheck.question: A tripeptide contains how many peptide bonds?
selfCheck.explanation: A chain of n amino acid residues has n - 1 peptide bonds, so a tripeptide has two.

selfCheck.question: What did Anfinsen's ribonuclease experiment show?
options: Proteins fold only with the help of chaperones
The amino acid sequence contains the information needed to specify the native fold
selfCheck.explanation: After denaturing and then removing the denaturant under gentle conditions, ribonuclease spontaneously refolded and regained activity, indicating that the sequence specifies the native structure.

selfCheck.question: In a folded water-soluble protein, where are non-polar side chains such as leucine most likely to be found?
selfCheck.explanation: The hydrophobic effect drives non-polar side chains into the interior, away from water, while polar and charged side chains tend to face the solvent.

units.title: Nucleic Acids and the Central Dogma
units.hook: Two strands, four letters, one rule of pairing: this simple scheme stores instructions for every protein you will ever make. When Watson and Crick showed how the structure of DNA suggested its own copying mechanism, they ended their paper with a famously understated sentence about it.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of a nucleotide, and distinguish DNA from RNA and purines from pyrimidines.
Explain 5' to 3' directionality, antiparallel strands and base pairing in the double helix.
Outline semi-conservative DNA replication and the roles of the three main RNA types.
Summarise the central dogma: transcription and translation, and the genetic code.
Give the scale of genomes and genes in bacteria and humans.

keyConcepts.definition: A nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and one or more phosphate groups; nucleotides are the monomers of nucleic acids and also act as energy carriers (ATP) and cofactors.
Purines (A, G) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one ring.
Sugars linked through phosphate groups between the 3' carbon of one nucleotide and the 5' carbon of the next, giving strands a direction (5' to 3').
A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds) in DNA; in RNA, A pairs with U.
Two antiparallel strands twisted around a common axis, with bases stacked inside, about 10 to 10.5 base pairs per turn in the B form, and major and minor grooves on the outside.
Each new DNA molecule contains one old and one newly synthesised strand, shown by the Meselson and Stahl experiment.
Information flows from DNA to RNA (transcription) to protein (translation); Crick's formulation says information cannot flow from protein back to nucleic acid, not that RNA to DNA is impossible.
Triplets of RNA bases (codons) specify amino acids: 64 codons, of which 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop signals; AUG is the start codon, and the code is redundant but not ambiguous.

deeper.beginner: DNA is a long molecule made from four building blocks (A, T, G, C). It forms a double helix in which A always pairs with T and G with C, which is why one strand can serve as the template for making the other. To make a protein, a cell copies a gene into messenger RNA (transcription), and the ribosome then reads the RNA three letters at a time to link amino acids in the right order (translation). That flow, DNA to RNA to protein, is the central dogma.
deeper.intermediate: RNA differs from DNA by having ribose (with a 2' hydroxyl), uracil instead of thymine, and usually being single-stranded; the 2' OH makes RNA more reactive and less stable, which suits a transient messenger. Strands are antiparallel: 5'-ATGC-3' pairs with 5'-GCAT-3'. Transcription is catalysed by RNA polymerase; in eukaryotes the primary transcript is processed (5' cap, splicing, poly-A tail). Translation uses mRNA, tRNAs (each carrying an amino acid and an anticodon) and rRNA in the ribosome, which is itself a ribozyme that forms the peptide bond. A human haploid genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs and about 20,000 protein-coding genes; the E. coli genome is about 4.6 million base pairs and about 4,300 genes.
deeper.advanced: Base stacking and hydrophobic effects contribute more to helix stability than hydrogen bonds alone, which is why the GC content alters the melting temperature but is not the whole story. DNA in cells is mostly B-form but can adopt A, Z and non-canonical forms such as G-quadruplexes, which have regulatory roles. The central dogma has recognised exceptions in the flow of information between nucleic acids: reverse transcription (retroviruses, telomerase, retrotransposons) and RNA replication in RNA viruses, but no case has been found of information passing from protein to protein or to nucleic acid, apart from the special case of prions where the information is conformational. Non-coding RNAs (microRNAs, lncRNAs) regulate genes, so the picture of RNA only as an intermediate is outdated.

commonMistakes: Writing U in DNA or T in RNA; remember T is DNA's, U is RNA's.
Reading a complementary strand in the same direction as the template; antiparallel strands mean you must reverse the sequence.
Saying the central dogma forbids RNA to DNA flow; it forbids flow from protein to nucleic acid.
Confusing codon (on mRNA) with anticodon (on tRNA), and gene (DNA) with the protein.

units.title: Membranes and Transport
units.hook: A cell is a chemical reaction kept alive by a barrier only two molecules thick. What passes through that barrier, and what is pumped across it against the odds, determines whether a cell lives, signals or dies.
learningObjectives: Describe the fluid mosaic model and the roles of lipids, cholesterol, proteins and carbohydrates in membranes.
Distinguish simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport and bulk transport.
Explain osmosis and predict cell behaviour in hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic solutions.
Describe the sodium-potassium pump and secondary active transport, and their role in establishing gradients.
Explain why membranes are selectively permeable using polarity and size.

keyConcepts.definition: The membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins float and move laterally, with different proteins and lipids on the two faces.
Integral proteins span or are embedded in the bilayer (often by alpha helices of hydrophobic residues); peripheral proteins attach to the surface.
Net movement of small, uncharged or non-polar molecules (O2, CO2, steroid hormones) down their concentration gradient directly through the lipid bilayer.
Passive movement of polar or charged molecules down their gradient through channel or carrier proteins (for example GLUT glucose transporters, aquaporins); no ATP is used.
Pumping substances against their gradient using ATP directly; the Na+/K+-ATPase exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP hydrolysed.
Using the stored energy of an ion gradient (usually Na+ or H+) to move another solute against its gradient, by symport or antiport.
Osmosis is the net movement of water across a semipermeable membrane toward the region of higher solute concentration; tonicity describes how an external solution affects cell volume.
The electrical voltage across the membrane produced by unequal ion distribution, typically about -70 mV (inside negative) in resting neurons.

deeper.beginner: The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids with proteins inserted in it. Small non-polar molecules slip through; ions and sugars cannot, so they need channels or carriers. Moving things down their gradient costs no energy, but moving them up needs pumps that use ATP. Water moves across membranes by osmosis toward the saltier side, so red blood cells swell in pure water and shrink in strong salt.
deeper.intermediate: Permeability depends on size, charge and polarity: O2, CO2 and ethanol cross easily; glucose, amino acids, Na+ and K+ essentially need proteins. Facilitated diffusion is saturable and specific (carriers) or gated (ion channels). The Na+/K+-ATPase maintains a high intracellular K+ and low Na+; the stored Na+ gradient drives secondary active transport, for example SGLT1 co-transports Na+ and glucose into intestinal cells. A cell in a hypotonic medium gains water and may swell and lyse (animal cells), while plant cells become turgid against the cell wall; in a hypertonic solution cells lose water and shrink (crenation, plasmolysis). Cholesterol keeps the membrane from being too fluid or too stiff, and lipid rafts are proposed to be small, dynamic, ordered domains enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids.
deeper.advanced: The Na+/K+-ATPase goes through the Post-Albers cycle with phosphorylated E1P and E2P intermediates, alternately exposing binding sites to the cytosol and to the outside; a large share of resting ATP use in neurons goes into maintaining these gradients. The electrochemical gradient of an ion combines concentration and voltage terms, delta mu = RT ln(c2/c1) + zF delta psi, which is why Na+ enters even when concentration alone would be balanced. Transporter kinetics follow Michaelis-Menten behaviour, while ion channels show rapid gating with single-channel conductances of picosiemens. Lipid rafts remain debated: they are best viewed as transient nanoscale assemblies rather than stable islands, and membrane protein function can also depend on specific lipid binding and bilayer thickness.

commonMistakes: Believing facilitated diffusion requires ATP; it is passive and follows the gradient.
Saying osmosis is movement of solute; it is movement of water.
Treating the membrane as static; proteins and lipids move laterally in the plane.
Forgetting that the Na+/K+ pump is electrogenic: 3 Na+ out and only 2 K+ in per cycle, contributing directly to the membrane potential.

units.title: The Endomembrane System, Protein Trafficking and the Cytoskeleton
units.hook: A pancreatic cell can produce a hormone, wrap it in a membrane bubble, tag it with a postal code and deliver it to the cell surface on cue. This internal logistics network, with its tracks and motors, shows the cell as an organised factory rather than a bag of enzymes.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure and function of the nucleus, rough and smooth ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes.
Trace a secreted protein from ribosome to plasma membrane, naming the signal sequence and vesicle steps.
Explain how lysosomes degrade material and why their pH matters.
Compare actin filaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules in structure and function.
Describe how motor proteins (kinesin, dynein, myosin) move cargo along cytoskeletal tracks.

keyConcepts.definition: A double membrane enclosing the nucleus and punctuated by nuclear pore complexes that regulate traffic of RNAs and proteins.
Rough ER has ribosomes and makes secreted and membrane proteins; smooth ER makes lipids, detoxifies compounds and stores calcium.
A short amino-terminal sequence recognised by the signal recognition particle that directs ribosomes making secretory proteins to the ER, where the chain is threaded into the lumen as it is made.
A stack of flattened cisternae that modifies (for example glycosylates), sorts and packages proteins and lipids arriving from the ER (cis face) for delivery (trans face).
Coated vesicles (COPII, COPI, clathrin) bud from one compartment and fuse with another, carrying cargo between organelles and to the plasma membrane.
An acidic organelle (pH about 4.5 to 5) containing hydrolytic enzymes that break down macromolecules, worn-out organelles and engulfed material.
Network of actin filaments (about 7 nm), intermediate filaments (about 10 nm) and microtubules (about 25 nm) giving shape, strength, intracellular transport and movement.
ATP-driven proteins that walk along filaments: kinesin toward the plus end of microtubules, dynein toward the minus end, and myosin along actin.

deeper.beginner: Inside a eukaryotic cell, membrane-wrapped compartments work as a production line. Proteins made on the rough ER are folded, sent in small bubbles (vesicles) to the Golgi, finished and labelled, then shipped to their destination, such as the cell surface or a lysosome. Meanwhile the cytoskeleton, a network of protein fibres, gives the cell its shape and acts as a railway for motor proteins that carry cargo.
deeper.intermediate: A protein with a signal peptide is recognised by SRP as it emerges from a free ribosome, which then docks on the ER membrane and translocates the chain into the lumen, where it folds and is often glycosylated. COPII vesicles carry cargo from ER to Golgi; COPI retrieves escaped ER proteins. The Golgi sorts cargo to lysosomes (via mannose-6-phosphate tags), to secretory vesicles, or to the plasma membrane. Lysosomal enzymes work optimally at acid pH, which protects the cell if one leaks into the neutral cytosol. Microtubules (alpha/beta tubulin dimers) radiate from a centrosome with minus ends anchored; kinesins carry vesicles toward the periphery, dynein carries them inward. Actin supports the cell cortex and movement, and intermediate filaments (keratins, lamins) give mechanical strength.
deeper.advanced: The signal hypothesis emerged from cell-free experiments showing that ER membranes and a signal sequence were enough to translocate a nascent chain. Sorting depends on nested coding: signal peptides, retention signals such as KDEL for ER-resident proteins, and mannose-6-phosphate for lysosomal enzymes; defects cause diseases such as I-cell disease. Microtubules show dynamic instability, alternating growth and shrinkage powered by GTP hydrolysis on beta-tubulin, which is exploited by anticancer drugs such as taxanes and vinca alkaloids. Autophagy, which delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes, links trafficking to quality control and metabolism, and endosomal sorting regulates how long receptors signal at the surface.

commonMistakes: Saying the Golgi makes proteins; proteins are made on ribosomes and modified and sorted in the Golgi.
Mixing up kinesin and dynein directions; kinesin generally runs to the plus end (outward), dynein to the minus end (toward the centre).
Thinking lysosomes work at neutral pH; their enzymes are acid hydrolases.
Treating the cytoskeleton as static scaffolding; it is continually assembled and disassembled.

units.title: Mitochondria, Chloroplasts and Cellular Energy
units.hook: Mitochondria carry their own DNA, divide like bacteria, and still cannot live without the cell that hosts them. They are the remnants of an ancient partnership, and the way they and chloroplasts turn electron flow into ATP is a story told in a single phrase: proton gradient.
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts and link structure to function.
Summarise the evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of these organelles.
Outline the stages of aerobic respiration and where each occurs.
Explain chemiosmosis: electron transport builds a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.
Give the overall inputs and outputs of the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

keyConcepts.definition: Adenosine triphosphate, the cell's energy currency: its hydrolysis to ADP and phosphate is coupled to unfavourable processes; it is continuously regenerated rather than stored.
A double-membrane organelle with a folded inner membrane (cristae) enclosing the matrix; site of the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
A double-membrane plastid containing stacks of thylakoid membranes (grana) in a fluid stroma; site of photosynthesis in plants and algae.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria engulfed by ancestral host cells, supported by their circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membranes and binary-fission-like division.
A series of membrane-bound complexes that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 to oxygen while pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The proton-motive force across the membrane drives protons back through ATP synthase, whose rotor turns to make ATP from ADP and phosphate.
In chloroplasts, light energy drives electron flow in the thylakoid membrane to make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to fix CO2 into sugars.
Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers phosphate directly from a substrate to ADP; oxidative phosphorylation uses the proton gradient produced by electron transport.

deeper.beginner: Cells need a steady supply of ATP. Mitochondria are the main ATP factories in animal and plant cells: they take fuel molecules derived from food and, using oxygen, release energy to make most of the cell's ATP. Chloroplasts in plants capture light energy to make sugars. Both organelles have two membranes and their own small DNA, which hints that they began as free-living bacteria.
deeper.intermediate: Glucose is broken down in glycolysis (cytosol) to pyruvate, which is converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidised in the citric acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix), yielding NADH and FADH2. Electrons from these carriers travel through complexes I to IV in the inner membrane to O2, forming water, while protons are pumped into the intermembrane space. The resulting gradient drives ATP synthase; a full oxidation of glucose yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP in current estimates (older textbooks say 36 to 38). In chloroplasts the same logic applies: light excites chlorophyll, electrons move through the thylakoid transport chain, protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen and ATP synthase makes ATP; the ATP and NADPH then power CO2 fixation by Rubisco in the Calvin cycle.
deeper.advanced: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis (1961) was initially controversial because it proposed that a proton gradient, not a high-energy chemical intermediate, couples electron transport to ATP synthesis; it was later confirmed and earned the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The proton-motive force has both an electrical (about 150 to 180 mV, inside negative) and a pH component. ATP synthase is a rotary motor: F0 rotation driven by protons turns the gamma subunit within F1, whose three catalytic sites cycle through binding, ATP formation and release; roughly 3 to 4 protons are needed per ATP including transport of phosphate. Mitochondria retain a small genome (human mtDNA is 16.6 kb, encoding 13 proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs), inherited maternally, and most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus, imported after synthesis. Uncoupling proteins can dissipate the gradient as heat, as in brown fat.

commonMistakes: Saying plants have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria; they have both, and respire as well as photosynthesise.
Using respiration as a synonym for breathing; cellular respiration is the biochemical oxidation of fuel.
Thinking ATP is stored in large amounts; it is turned over rapidly (a person recycles roughly their own body weight in ATP per day).
Believing the electron transport chain itself makes ATP; it builds the proton gradient, and ATP synthase makes ATP.

units.title: Cell Signalling and Communication
units.hook: Adrenaline reaches a liver cell at nanomolar concentrations and, within seconds, the cell releases glucose into the blood, an effect millions of times larger than the signal that triggered it. How a tiny signal at the surface becomes a big response inside is the essence of cell signalling.
learningObjectives: Describe the three stages of signalling: reception, transduction and response.
Compare endocrine, paracrine, autocrine and juxtacrine signalling.
Identify the main receptor classes and give examples (GPCRs, receptor tyrosine kinases, ion channels, nuclear receptors).
Explain the roles of second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+, IP3, DAG) and of kinase cascades in amplification.
Explain how signals are terminated and why that matters.

keyConcepts.definition: A ligand is the signalling molecule; the receptor is the protein that binds it specifically, and binding changes the receptor's conformation or activity.
The chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular response.
A seven-transmembrane receptor that activates a heterotrimeric G protein, which then regulates enzymes such as adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C.
A receptor that dimerises on ligand binding and phosphorylates itself on tyrosines, creating docking sites for signalling proteins (for example the insulin and EGF receptors).
A small intracellular molecule or ion produced or released after receptor activation, such as cAMP, Ca2+, IP3 and DAG, that spreads and amplifies the signal.
A sequence in which each activated kinase phosphorylates the next, so a single receptor event is amplified many thousand-fold.
Receptors for lipid-soluble ligands, such as steroid hormones, that act directly on gene transcription after the hormone crosses the membrane.
Switching signals off by degrading ligands, GTP hydrolysis by G proteins, phosphodiesterases breaking down cAMP, and phosphatases removing phosphate.

deeper.beginner: Cells talk to each other with chemical messages. A message molecule binds a specific receptor, usually on the surface; the receptor then sets off a chain of events inside the cell that changes what the cell does. Each step can amplify the signal. Some messages, such as steroid hormones, are fat-soluble and slip through the membrane to bind receptors inside.
deeper.intermediate: In the adrenaline pathway, adrenaline binds a beta-adrenergic receptor (a GPCR); the receptor activates Gs, which exchanges GDP for GTP and stimulates adenylyl cyclase to make cAMP; cAMP activates protein kinase A, which sets off a cascade that activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthesis, releasing glucose. Termination comes from GTP hydrolysis by the G protein, cAMP breakdown by phosphodiesterase, and phosphatases. Receptor tyrosine kinases trigger the Ras and MAP kinase cascade and PI3K pathways controlling growth and survival. Calcium is a second messenger released from the ER through IP3-gated channels; it binds proteins such as calmodulin.
deeper.advanced: Signalling networks show features such as ultrasensitivity (switch-like responses from multisite phosphorylation), feedback loops that generate oscillations or bistability, and crosstalk between pathways. Specificity is achieved by scaffold proteins and spatial compartmentalisation (for example A-kinase anchoring proteins organising PKA). Receptor desensitisation by GPCR kinases and arrestins both stops signalling and initiates alternative signalling. Many drugs target these systems: a large fraction of drugs act on GPCRs, and kinase inhibitors such as imatinib exploit dependencies on constitutively active kinases in cancers. Mutations in signalling proteins (such as Ras, mutated in a large share of human tumours) lock pathways on, linking this unit to the cell-cycle unit that follows.

commonMistakes: Saying the signalling molecule enters the cell and carries the message; for surface receptors the ligand stays outside and the receptor passes on the information.
Confusing the first messenger (the extracellular ligand) with the second messenger (an intracellular molecule such as cAMP).
Forgetting that signals must be switched off; failure to terminate (for example cholera toxin keeping Gs active) causes disease.
Treating phosphorylation as always activating; it can activate or inhibit depending on the protein.

units.title: The Cell Cycle, Division and Cell Death
units.hook: You began as a single cell and now contain tens of trillions, and nearly every one was produced by the same tightly regulated loop of growth and division. When the brakes on that loop fail, the result is cancer, and when the cell chooses to self-destruct, the result is sculpted tissue: the webbing between fingers vanished this way.
learningObjectives: Describe the phases of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, M) and the stages of mitosis.
Explain the role of cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints in cell-cycle control.
Compare mitosis and meiosis and explain how meiosis generates genetic diversity.
Describe apoptosis, how it differs from necrosis, and its role in development.
Explain in outline how loss of cell-cycle control contributes to cancer.

keyConcepts.definition: Interphase (G1 growth, S DNA synthesis, G2 preparation) followed by M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis); non-dividing cells may exit to G0.
Nuclear division producing two genetically identical nuclei: prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, usually followed by cytokinesis.
After S phase each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere; they separate at anaphase and become independent chromosomes.
Cyclin-dependent kinases are active only when bound to a cyclin whose levels rise and fall through the cycle, driving transitions between phases.
Control points (G1/S, G2/M and the spindle assembly checkpoint) that halt the cycle if DNA is damaged or chromosomes are incorrectly attached.
Two successive divisions after one round of DNA replication, producing four haploid cells; crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation.
Regulated cell death executed by caspase enzymes, producing orderly cell shrinkage and packaging that does not trigger inflammation, unlike necrosis.
Tumour suppressors (such as p53 and Rb) restrain cycle progression and promote repair or death; oncogenes (such as mutant Ras) drive growth, and cancer usually requires several such changes.

deeper.beginner: Cells divide in a repeating cycle: grow, copy their DNA, check everything, then split into two identical daughter cells. During mitosis the copied chromosomes line up and are pulled apart so each new cell gets a full set. Special divisions called meiosis make sperm and egg cells with half the usual chromosome number. Cells also have a built-in self-destruct programme, apoptosis, used to remove damaged or unneeded cells.
deeper.intermediate: A human cell has 46 chromosomes; after S phase there are 46 chromosomes each made of two sister chromatids. In anaphase the chromatids separate, so each daughter gets 46. Cyclin-CDK complexes drive phase transitions: cyclin D-CDK4/6 and cyclin E-CDK2 push cells through G1/S by phosphorylating Rb, and cyclin B-CDK1 triggers mitosis. p53 detects DNA damage, stops the cycle (via p21) and can trigger apoptosis. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair and swap segments in prophase I (crossing over), separate in meiosis I, and sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, giving four genetically distinct haploid cells. Apoptosis involves initiator and executioner caspases activated through the intrinsic (mitochondrial, cytochrome c) or extrinsic (death receptor) pathway.
deeper.advanced: Hartwell's checkpoint work in yeast and Nurse's discovery of CDK as a universal M-phase control, both recognised by the 2001 Nobel Prize, established the idea of the cell cycle as a series of regulated dependencies rather than a clock. The spindle assembly checkpoint blocks anaphase until all kinetochores are attached to microtubules, preventing aneuploidy. Cancer arises from accumulated mutations and epigenetic changes: Hanahan and Weinberg's hallmarks include sustained proliferative signalling, evasion of growth suppressors, resisting cell death, enabling replicative immortality, inducing angiogenesis and activating invasion, with later additions of metabolic reprogramming and immune evasion. Therapeutic strategies exploit these dependencies: CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer, microtubule poisons that trigger the spindle checkpoint, and drugs that restore apoptosis such as BCL-2 inhibitors.

commonMistakes: Confusing chromosome number with chromatid number after S phase; DNA content doubles but chromosome number stays 46 until anaphase.
Mixing up mitosis and meiosis outcomes: mitosis gives two diploid identical cells, meiosis gives four haploid different cells.
Calling apoptosis 'cell damage'; it is an active, controlled programme, whereas necrosis is accidental and messy.
Saying cancer is caused by a single mutation; it typically requires an accumulation of changes in several genes.
